In order to support the high power and wideband waveforms, the phased-array antenna is broken into subarrays, each with a time delay unit (TDU) and final power amplifier. The use of wideband LFM pulses causes significant problems in terms of frequency dispersion if the antenna is a phased array. The effects of wideband LFM signal processing in phased array radars have been documented in the past [1]. Further work was performed [2] which addressed the particular issues associated with a subarrayed phased-array antenna as might be required in a wide bandwidth, high gain system. In addition to the performance issues of dispersion loss, compressed pulse widths, and grating lobes, the use of quantized TDU's causes a degradation of the null depth in monopulse systems.

articleTitle: New formulations for mutual coupling computations of antennas on general quadric cylinders and surfaces of revolution
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: Microstrip and slot antennas are often used in aerospace vehicles because of their advantages of simplicity in construction, lightweight and their ability to conform to the shape of the space-borne structures. In practice, a large number of aerospace bodies or their significantly scattering portions can be conveniently approximated by Quadric Surfaces of Revolution (QUASORs) or Quadric Cylinders (QUACYLs). The theoretical performance of the antennas in presence of these structures is amenable to analysis using the ray-theoretic techniques such as the Uniform Theory of Diffraction (UTD).

articleTitle: Characterization techniques of single-mode fibers
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to review the recent developments of single mode fiber testing methods currently being used by the fiber optics industry. Each test method will be discussed in terms of the relevance of the parameter being measured, precision and speed. In addition, future trends on fiber optics communication systems have dictated the characterization of new parameters and the generation of new fiber types. These measurements will be discussed briefly in this paper.

articleTitle: Circular Polarized Antennas Employing Linearly Polarized Radiators
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: Circularly polarized antennas are commonly designed using two different approaches: 1) by shaping the geometry, and 2) by dual excitation of linearly polarized antennas. The most common antennas of the first type are the helical antennas, where the radiation is due to a circulating electric current on the conducting wire of the antenna. The geometry of the antenna controls the polarization and as such the radiation is either a right hand or a left hand circular polarization, depending on the helix sense of rotation. The polarization diversity is often impossible, although it may be achieved in some applications by feeding the antenna at the opposite end. Circular polarization is also achievable in travelling wave antennas by controlling the radiation zone and radiating current phase. The second antenna types are often symmetric in geometry such as horns or microstrip patches, where the circular polarization is achieved by a dual feed configuration or a deformation of the geometry to excite, at a phase quadrature, the required orthogonal modes.

articleTitle: Analysis of planar opto-etectromagnetic structures using the finite-difference time-domain method
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: The finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method [1] is used to analyze wave propagating in dielectric-slab optical waveguides. Unlike other methods which assume small reflections and can only study weakly guided or canonical structures. The time explicit FDTD method makes few assumption and can be used to analyze structures with arbitrary geometry and large refractive index mismatches. Excellent agreement with the exact solution in beat lengths and field distribution has been found for the parallel symmetrical slab problem. The implementation of the method is discussed, and the utility of this method in integrated optical waveguide analysis is illustrated.

articleTitle: Scattering from surface impedance sphere coated with dielectric materials
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: An exact solution of surface impedance sphere coated with dielectric materials is presented in Mie series form. The solution accuracy is verified by comparing with other exact formulations as well as the numerical solution based on the method of moments. Different numerical examples are presented in order to illustrate the effect of the material types on the scattered fields.

articleTitle: The WATMIC — A software that treats microwave integrated circuits like linear antennas
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: Without the dielectric substrate, a microwave integrated circuit is equivalent to a complex linear antenna (passive or active) backed by a ground plane. The “MIC-Antenna”. fortunately, does not have significant radiation due to its small size.

articleTitle: The magnetostatic dipole inversion problem in remote sensing
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: The static magnetic dipole inversion problem is related to the problem of location and identification of compact ferrous objects. It is shown that the inversion of the dipole field or gradient is a necessary first step toward determining object location and identity. Several recursive and nonrecursive methods of determining dipole moment and location from field or gradient measurements are described and compared. It is shown that given dipole moment estimates, it is possible to determine the identity of the dipole source in practical situations by pattern recognition.

articleTitle: Radar crosssection of dielectric bodies with partially thin conducitng coatins
publicationTitle: 1988 Symposium on Antenna Technology and Applied Electromagnetics
abstract: The scattering of electromagnetic waves from axisynmetric bodies, partially coated with a thin metallic layer is considered. The aim is to study the general properties of the scattering process from such complex targets for which analytic and experimental results are needed, and also to investigate the effect of metallic coating on the radar signature of these targets. The scattering problem is formulated in terms of equivalent currents on the surface of the scatterer, leading to surface integral equations which are solved using the method of moments. Monostatic measurements of the polarimetric matrix are carried out at 9.6 GHG using circular polarization. Very good agreement between tie experimental data and the numerical results, for a wide variety of target configurations, is obtained.
